title: Planning for Dunkelflaute: NESO on system risk, options and timescales
label: 28 October 2026 · Dunkelflaute and intermittency
summary: Julian Leslie of the National Energy System Operator (NESO) told the Lords committee how NESO models rare low-wind, low-sun events (Dunkelflaute), what long-term options it has proposed to Government, and how it balances security, cost and net zero. NESO has produced six whole‑system pathways to 2050 and says all meet legally binding carbon targets and reliability standards, but the Government must choose a pathway so investors can act. NESO described technical fixes (synchronous condensers, grid‑forming inverters, batteries), reliance on dispatchable generation (including unabated gas for now), the role of interconnectors, and accepted recent recommendations on internal governance and communications.

speakers.label: Julian Leslie
speakers.name: Julian Leslie
speakers.role: Chief Engineer and Director of Strategic Energy Planning, NESO

glossary.definition: A weather spell with very low wind and low sunlight, so wind and solar produce little electricity.
Power plants that can be turned on when needed, for example gas plants, hydrogen turbines or plants with carbon capture.
A machine that gives the grid rotational inertia needed to keep frequency stable when big generators are absent.
Power electronics that let batteries and renewables behave like traditional generators to stabilise the grid.
NESO's government-commissioned, whole‑system plan mapping generation, storage and network needs through to 2050.
A reliability measure set by Government that estimates expected hours per year without enough supply; UK standard is three hours.
An electricity link between countries that lets Britain import or export power.
A Government-run market that pays providers to be available in future years to secure supply.
NESO's earlier advice and Government action plan setting generation requirements to 2030.

chapters.title: How NESO thinks about Dunkelflaute
chapters.takeaway: NESO models many weather scenarios, including long low‑wind/low‑sun periods, and plans to guarantee supply first while balancing cost and net zero.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Please introduce yourself and tell us how NESO defines Dunkelflaute and what assumptions you use for wind and solar output.

turns.speaker: Julian Leslie
turns.text: I lead strategic energy planning at NESO. We treat Dunkelflaute as one of many weather extremes. We use 40-plus years of weather data and Met Office work (project UNSEEN) to test extremes, not averages. Security of supply is the priority in all our analysis.

turns.speaker: Julian Leslie
turns.text: When renewables are very low we assume reduced outputs for wind and solar and plan where the energy must come from instead. Today that back-up is mainly unabated gas; in future it could be hydrogen-to-power or gas with carbon capture.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Are you giving the Government clear options and timescales so investors can act?

turns.speaker: Julian Leslie
turns.text: Yes. We published Clean Power 2030 advice and six Strategic Spatial Energy Plan pathways that show technologies, volumes, timing and locations to 2050. Each pathway aims to be secure, low‑carbon and costed; the Secretary of State must now choose which to follow.

chapters.title: The Strategic Spatial Energy Plan and who decides
chapters.takeaway: NESO produced six whole‑system pathways; it advises but does not set policy—the Government and regulator decide which pathway to adopt, which then guides investment.

turns.speaker: Lord Lennie
turns.text: Can NESO or Government set clearer targets for storage and low‑carbon dispatchable tech for Dunkelflaute?

turns.speaker: Julian Leslie
turns.text: The SSEP pathways set the volumes and timing for different technologies. Which pathway is chosen determines the required mix—more nuclear means less storage, more floating offshore wind means more storage.

turns.speaker: Lord Krebs
turns.text: What's the difference between your published future scenarios and these six strategic options?

turns.speaker: Julian Leslie
turns.text: Our future scenarios outline possible futures. The SSEP pathways are a co‑optimised, geospatial, deliverability‑focused plan commissioned by Government—designed to be actionable across planning, networks and markets.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Do the pathways meet the Climate Change Committee's carbon budgets?

turns.speaker: Julian Leslie
turns.text: Yes—the SSEP pathways meet government targets and net zero by 2050; our longer‑term future scenarios mostly meet budgets, with one falling short.

turns.speaker: Lord Jay of Ewelme
turns.text: Will having a government‑approved SSEP give investors the certainty they need?

turns.speaker: Julian Leslie
turns.text: That is the aim: a Government‑approved plan, endorsed by the regulator and used in planning decisions and pricing reform, gives long‑term clarity for supply chains and skills investment.

chapters.title: Technical fixes for system stability and costs
chapters.takeaway: NESO says synchronous condensers, grid‑forming inverters and batteries can replace inertia and stabilize the grid, likely cheaper than running extra gas capacity—cost estimates will be supplied in writing.

turns.speaker: Lord Redwood
turns.text: To run lots of wind and solar you need synchronous condensers and grid‑forming inverters; what scale and cost are we talking about?

turns.speaker: Julian Leslie
turns.text: We have already procured condensers and grid‑forming inverters with batteries to replace lost inertia. Buying those services is relatively low cost and reduces the need to run gas plants; cost‑benefit favours these investments.

turns.speaker: Lord Redwood
turns.text: I heard a condenser can be £50–100m and we might need many—can you confirm?

turns.speaker: Julian Leslie
turns.text: I'll provide detailed cost and numbers in writing, but the headline is these measures displace the need to run large gas units and are cheaper across the system.

turns.speaker: Lord Trees
turns.text: Is there a 'sweet spot' for how much wind or solar is optimal given storage and dispatchable costs?

turns.speaker: Julian Leslie
turns.text: There is no single answer: the optimal mix depends on the full pathway—nuclear, storage and demand flexibility all change the arithmetic. That's precisely what the SSEP maps out.

chapters.title: Reliability, interconnectors and demand response
chapters.takeaway: NESO stresses high reliability today, treats interconnectors as valuable but derated in stress cases, and sees demand‑side measures and home batteries as growing contributors.

turns.speaker: Lord Ashcombe
turns.text: You said Britain is very reliable. How do you measure that, and what if interconnectors stop delivering?

turns.speaker: Julian Leslie
turns.text: We use loss of supply metrics. I quoted reliability figures—99.69% and a separate point that 99.9996% of power is delivered—those are how we express performance. Interconnectors are crucial and give low‑cost flexibility, but we derate them in capacity planning so we don't rely on full import in stress events.

turns.speaker: Lord Ashcombe
turns.text: Roughly how much do interconnectors supply?

turns.speaker: Julian Leslie
turns.text: Around 10% in some years, but it varies. We have correlation analyses per interconnector and can share details in writing.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Can NESO influence public behaviour to smooth peaks, and can household batteries be used for longer events?

turns.speaker: Julian Leslie
turns.text: Suppliers already use flexibility offers and reward customers to shift demand—millions participate. Clean Power 2030 assumed about 12 GW of demand flexibility by 2030. Household batteries and thermal stores will play a larger role as markets develop.

chapters.title: Governance, the Eversheds report and delivery timelines
chapters.takeaway: NESO welcomed an independent Eversheds review, is acting on recommendations, delivered the SSEP to the Secretary of State in August, expects a decision soon, and plans public consultation in 2027.

turns.speaker: Baroness McIntosh of Pickering
turns.text: Is Britain on track to deliver the capacity needed for a range of Dunkelflaute events, and which technologies should be prioritised?

turns.speaker: Julian Leslie
turns.text: Today's system is highly resilient. The SSEP sets what to deliver and when, recognising lead times—some technologies take many years to build. The plan tells government and markets when decisions must be made to meet 2050.

turns.speaker: Baroness McIntosh of Pickering
turns.text: The Eversheds report criticised internal culture and control‑room communications—how are you responding?

turns.speaker: Julian Leslie
turns.text: We welcome the report, have accepted its recommendations and are working on action plans. Our planning for system security remains rigorous and our capacity mechanisms and market rules provide back‑up.

turns.speaker: Baroness Whitaker
turns.text: Could better-targeted subsidy speed up technologies like tidal?

turns.speaker: Julian Leslie
turns.text: The SSEP is updated every three years. If tidal or other tech become affordable and deliverable, future plans will include them. Government decides which tech to support.

turns.speaker: Baroness Coffey
turns.text: Why wasn't there more local capacity near London when the system needed emergency assistance?

turns.speaker: Julian Leslie
turns.text: Network design balances flows, cost, deliverability and environmental impact. Sometimes a circuit is out or maintenance is happening. The SSEP will inform the central network plan so future network upgrades match the chosen pathway.

turns.speaker: Baroness Rafferty
turns.text: Are there enough skilled workers to build the networks you describe?

turns.speaker: Julian Leslie
turns.text: Skills and supply‑chain capacity are a real challenge. One aim of an approved long‑term plan is to give firms confidence to invest in training and manufacturing here.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Who set the SSEP timetable and is it fast enough?

turns.speaker: Julian Leslie
turns.text: Government commissioned the work; new data a year into the project required rework. We delivered the six pathways to the Secretary of State in August and expect a decision later this year. The chosen pathway will be consulted on through 2027.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you—we look forward to the decision and expect NESO to help speed delivery so security isn't compromised.

turns.speaker: Julian Leslie
turns.text: We will. Our job is to plan and advise; policy and procurement decisions sit with Government and the regulator. Our analyses are designed to keep the lights on while meeting net zero affordably.
